choices.text: Book the DFW nonstop plus drive, and use that same large-airport-plus-car approach whenever a smaller airport needs a connection.
Book ACT because the destination airport should lead whenever it is closest to the site, even if the last regional leg is thin.
Lead with DFW here: it protects Tuesday with daylight driving and recovery options; keep ACT only if the connection gets materially safer.
Pick AUS on fare if the rental day and mileage keep total cost lowest; treat the three airports as fare equivalents.

probes.difficulty_rationale: DFW plus driving resembles tempting prior large-airport wins, while ACT sounds natural because it is closest. The chosen policy picks a route-specific winner without turning either pattern into an all-trip rule.
probes.gold_action: Lead with DFW for this Waco trip because the schedule, drive timing, and recovery options protect Tuesday better than ACT or AUS.
probes.label_rationale: Past airport decisions split across larger alternates and closer fields: Boise and ABQ were selected for reliability, while ORF, MDT, and Pasco won when drive or first-site timing mattered. DFW is justified here only by the Waco schedule and recovery margin.
probes.query: Upcoming: SFO to Waco for a Tuesday 9:30 a.m. plant walk. ACT via DFW arrives Monday 8:45 p.m. on a thin regional last leg; DFW nonstop arrives 2:10 p.m. with a 1h45 daylight drive and more later arrivals; AUS is $90 cheaper but a 2h45 drive near dusk. Which airport policy fits?

choices.text: Book MSP whenever it offers a nonstop; the larger airport plus car is the standard hedge against regional connections.
Book DLH for this trip because it avoids the winter night drive and still has a same-day backup leg.
Book whichever option is cheapest after adding the rental, since DLH and MSP both reach the site Tuesday.
Book DLH on every Duluth-area trip because the closest airport should always beat a Minneapolis drive.

probes.difficulty_rationale: MSP is plausibly attractive as the nonstop, and DLH is plausibly attractive as the closest field. The distractors overstate each attraction into a fixed airport strategy.
probes.gold_action: Use DLH for this Duluth trip because the current backup leg and winter ground risk make the local airport the more reliable door-to-door plan.
probes.label_rationale: The cited trips include both larger-airport wins and local-airport wins. DLH wins here because the current winter drive and backup-leg facts outweigh the MSP nonstop, not because closest airports should always dominate.
probes.query: SFO to Duluth for a Wednesday 8:00 a.m. safety gate in January. DLH via MSP arrives Tuesday 4:25 p.m.; if the last leg misconnects there is a 9:40 p.m. backup. MSP nonstop arrives Tuesday 2:00 p.m. but creates a 2.5-hour snowy/dark drive. Which airport policy fits?

choices.text: Book CHO because the closest airport should anchor the plan when the first site is in Charlottesville.
Book IAD nonstop and drive; avoid small destination airports whenever a reliable nonstop exists nearby.
Lead with RIC here: it gives earlier arrival, manageable driving, and recovery margin without the late CHO regional.
Rank by airfare after removing options that arrive after midnight; ground time is secondary once arrival is Monday.

probes.difficulty_rationale: CHO, IAD, and RIC each have an apparent advantage, so a simplistic closest-airport, largest-airport, or fare-filter policy can look defensible. The chosen policy uses the current route mix.
probes.gold_action: Lead with RIC for this Charlottesville trip because it balances arrival time, drive exposure, and connection risk better than CHO or IAD.
probes.label_rationale: The evidence supports door-to-door comparison rather than airport-size loyalty: some alternates won for connection reliability, while ORF, MDT, and Pasco won when the drive or early commitment changed the risk.
probes.query: SFO to Charlottesville for a Tuesday 1:00 p.m. campus walkthrough. CHO via IAD arrives Monday 11:20 p.m. on a late regional; RIC arrives 3:30 p.m. with a 1h10 drive; IAD nonstop arrives 4:45 p.m. with a 2h15 drive through DC traffic. Which airport policy fits?

choices.text: Book Sunday night now for any install trip, since badge or crate work usually rewards arriving a day early.
Book Monday only; approval controls early arrivals even if the badge time changes.
Make Monday noon the base and keep a cancellable Sunday-arrival option until badge and approval decisions land.
Fly Monday evening and skip any hold; only the confirmed Tuesday task should drive cost.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Sunday-now echoes prior protected setups, while Monday-only echoes trips where earlier nights were cut. The chosen policy separates the unconfirmed badge risk from a routine extra-night habit.
probes.gold_action: Use Monday noon as the base plan and hold a cancellable Sunday-arrival option only while the Monday badge pickup and approval remain unsettled.
probes.label_rationale: Earlier arrivals were added for concrete access, crate, and inspection risks, then removed or avoided when those risks disappeared or cost approval did not support them. The Salt Lake facts call for a temporary held structure.
probes.query: Salt Lake City install: the first confirmed task is Tuesday 9:00 a.m.; the vendor may add a Monday 8:00 a.m. badge pickup, and finance has not approved Sunday hotel yet. Monday flights reach SLC by noon with many backups. Which arrival policy fits?

choices.text: Arrive Sunday for all conference setups, so any booth issue can be handled a full day early.
Arrive Monday evening; skip Sunday because the first obligation is Tuesday afternoon and no freight risk is assigned.
Fly Tuesday morning only, since setup is not until 3:00 p.m. and an extra hotel night is wasteful.
Wait to book all travel until the exhibitor packet is final, even if Monday fares rise.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A Sunday conference buffer and a same-day Tuesday flight both sound plausible from prior patterns. The chosen plan uses the current setup window rather than a standing conference-arrival rule.
probes.gold_action: Book a Monday evening Atlanta arrival and no Sunday night because the current setup time and lack of freight duty leave adequate margin.
probes.label_rationale: The cited trips show Sunday was useful when crate checks or inspections created a hard Monday risk, while later setups and Nashville-style timing supported dropping Sunday. This Atlanta setup has no Monday gate or freight exposure.
probes.query: Atlanta conference: booth setup is Tuesday 3:00-6:00 p.m.; there is no freight or crate responsibility, no Monday meeting, hotel rates spike Sunday, and Monday evening arrivals are reliable. The organizer suggests a Sunday arrival like other exhibitors. Which arrival policy fits?

choices.text: Arrive Sunday for this trip because Monday crate verification and Tuesday's early run-through leave little recovery room.
Use Monday travel because the official customer session is Tuesday; the branch can check crates if needed.
Arrive Sunday for every distributor or setup trip, even if crates and access later move to Tuesday.
Fly Monday morning on the earliest nonstop and have branch staff sign crates if delays occur.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Both Sunday and early Monday travel are operationally plausible. The distractors convert a crate-buffer pattern or a cost-saving pattern into a broad rule, while the chosen plan keys off the current Monday verification duty.
probes.gold_action: Arrive Sunday for the Milwaukee trip because Monday crate verification and the Tuesday early run-through create a specific protected-access risk.
probes.label_rationale: Specific crate checks, inspections, and access windows supported early arrival in cited trips, while other cited trips rejected Sunday when the risk moved later or disappeared. Milwaukee has the concrete risk.
probes.query: Milwaukee distributor training: Monday 4:00 p.m. demo-room unlock and Tuesday 7:30 a.m. customer run-through. The demo crates arrive Monday morning and the branch asks the user to verify them before close. Sunday hotel is approved. Which arrival policy fits?

choices.text: Stay downtown whenever there is a decent restaurant scene; morning drives can be handled with an early departure.
Stay near Westlake/Elyria for this trip, prioritizing parking and the early plant gate over downtown evenings.
Stay by CLE airport as a general compromise for all Cleveland-area work, regardless of site side.
Use the client's downtown preferred hotel whenever offered, even if the first gate is suburban.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Downtown and airport bases are both plausible generic work-trip choices. The chosen policy does not make non-downtown hotels universal; it applies the current early gate and parking facts.
probes.gold_action: Book the Westlake/Elyria-area hotel for this Cleveland trip because the early plant gate and parking needs dominate the hotel geography.
probes.label_rationale: The cited stays alternate between plant-side practicality and central walkable locations. This Cleveland case matches the industrial-park and plant-drive episodes more than the leisure, downtown, or convention cases.
probes.query: Cleveland trip: Tuesday 7:15 a.m. gate at an Elyria plant, rental car required, no scheduled downtown dinners, and the team offers either a well-rated Crocker Park/Westlake hotel with parking or a downtown lakefront hotel. Which hotel-location policy fits?

choices.text: Book the River Walk/convention-area hotel because this trip values walkability and evening plans over parking.
Book the airport hotel whenever rideshare is easy; central hotels are usually unnecessary.
Book a suburban plant-side hotel by default for work trips, then rideshare into the meeting.
Use only official-block hotels for conferences; if full, wait for cancellations before booking elsewhere.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A cheaper airport hotel and an official-block rule are plausible conference shortcuts, and a plant-side rule echoes other work trips. The chosen policy follows this trip's evening and no-car constraints.
probes.gold_action: Book the River Walk or convention-area hotel for this San Antonio trip because walkability, spouse evenings, and no rental car drive the geography.
probes.label_rationale: Central hotels won in cited leisure, evening-heavy, and convention contexts, while plant-side hotels won for early industrial access. San Antonio aligns with the walkable conference and spouse-evening side of that split.
probes.query: San Antonio trip: three-night industry meeting at the convention center, spouse joins for evenings, no rental car is planned, and the official block is full. Options include a River Walk hotel with better reviews or a cheaper airport hotel with parking. Which hotel-location policy fits?

choices.text: Stay downtown all nights; multi-night trips should favor restaurants and reception access.
Book Garner for Monday/Tuesday and downtown for Wednesday, matching the early plant and reception nights.
Stay RTP airport all nights; a midpoint base avoids over-weighting either plant or reception.
Stay Garner all nights; for work travel, plant-side parking should beat evening plans.

probes.difficulty_rationale: All-night downtown, all-night plant-side, and airport-midpoint policies each echo plausible prior outcomes. The chosen policy avoids turning either hotel geography into a blanket work-trip preference.
probes.gold_action: Use a split stay: Garner for the early plant portion and downtown Raleigh for the reception night.
probes.label_rationale: The cited hotel choices reverse with trip purpose: plant access and parking pushed suburban, while evenings, conventions, and personal time pushed central. Raleigh contains both pressures, so the geography should change with the itinerary.
probes.query: Raleigh trip: Monday night arrival, Tuesday 7:30 a.m. plant meeting in Garner, Wednesday reception downtown, and Thursday airport departure. Hotels under consideration are downtown Raleigh, RTP airport, or a Garner hotel with parking. Which location policy fits?

choices.text: Use no rental car; rely on transit or rideshare unless a site visit is added.
Book a compact SUV for every work trip, since site roads and cargo can appear late.
Book a compact car by default; even city conferences need flexible movement after hours.
Open a company-portal compact reservation now, even though no car is currently planned.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Compact and compact-SUV defaults are tempting from plant trips, while portal handling can sound administratively safe. The chosen policy follows the current no-site urban setup.
probes.gold_action: Leave the rental car unset for this Boston conference and use transit or rideshare unless a site visit is added.
probes.label_rationale: The cited trips include no-car urban and conference plans, compact rentals for ordinary mobility, and compact SUVs for rain or plant-road needs. Boston has no site visit, no cargo, and expensive parking.
probes.query: Boston trip: two nights at a Back Bay conference hotel, no customer site visit, demo gear is carry-on, parking is $58 per night, and airport-to-hotel transit is straightforward. Which ground-transport policy fits?

choices.text: Book a compact SUV at BTR; it fits the gear and wet lot without moving up to full-size.
Use rideshare as city work trips often work fine without a car.
Book a compact car for every ordinary solo trip, even with light gear and bad weather.
Book a full-size SUV whenever a plant or gravel lot is involved.

probes.difficulty_rationale: No-car and compact-car policies echo other trips, and a full-size SUV sounds protective for gravel. The chosen option uses the current site-road and gear facts rather than a fixed class.
probes.gold_action: Book a compact SUV for this Baton Rouge audit because gear, rain, and gravel justify more clearance without requiring a full-size SUV.
probes.label_rationale: Prior ground plans ranged from no rental to compact cars to compact SUVs. This current audit resembles the rain and plant-road case, while still supporting the smallest class that fits the conditions.
probes.query: Baton Rouge plant audit: the hotel is 35 minutes from the site, the user carries PPE plus a calibration case, rain is forecast, and the plant's overflow lot uses gravel. Which rental policy fits?

choices.text: Book a National compact car; it covers the site commute without paying for a larger class.
Skip the rental for all training trips and rely on rideshare unless someone adds a plant tour.
Book a compact SUV for work trips because weather, lots, or PPE may become issues.
Leave the car out and handle rentals separately through the company portal every time.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Rideshare-only, compact-SUV, and separate-portal policies all match some prior travel outcomes. The chosen policy keeps the rental class tied to this trip's simple site commute.
probes.gold_action: Book a compact car for this Madison training because a car is useful for the campus commute, but the gear and road conditions do not justify an SUV.
probes.label_rationale: The cited episodes show rentals depend on site access, cargo, weather, and transit practicality. Madison needs a car for the client-campus commute, but it does not have the conditions that justified a compact SUV elsewhere.
probes.query: Madison training: the site is 25 minutes from MSN, the hotel is near the client campus, there is no demo case beyond a laptop bag, roads are paved and clear, and evening parking is included. Which rental policy fits?

choices.text: Ship these small non-hazmat boxes to the confirmed hotel reservation and note pickup at check-in.
Ship all work materials to the hotel by default, even before package policies are checked.
Route every box through the decorator or local branch, avoiding hotel receiving for all work items.
Carry the scanner kit and check the literature box on the flight, avoiding third-party receiving.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hotel routing is tempting because it has worked for small packages, while decorator or carry-on routing sounds safer from other episodes. The chosen policy applies only to the confirmed package facts here.
probes.gold_action: Ship the small non-hazmat Indianapolis boxes to the hotel because the front desk has confirmed holding under the reservation.
probes.label_rationale: Hotel receiving was used in cited sessions only after confirming package size, hazmat limits, and reservation details; other cited sessions used carry-on, decorator, trailer, or dock routing. Indianapolis meets the small confirmed-hotel case.
probes.query: Indianapolis conference: one small scanner kit and a 12-pound literature box need to arrive two days early. The hotel front desk confirms package holding with the user's reservation number and no hazmat; decorator receiving is expensive. Which shipping policy fits?

choices.text: Ship the crate to the show decorator using dock labels and pickup hours for this event.
Send it to the hotel anyway; hotels are the simplest holding point for arriving travelers.
Send it to the nearest distributor branch for every trade show, then courier it across town.
Have the user check the crate as baggage whenever hotel receiving is limited.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hotel and branch routing both sound familiar from prior logistics, and checking baggage may look simple. The chosen policy keys off crate weight, show-floor timing, and confirmed decorator receiving.
probes.gold_action: Ship the Houston crate to the show decorator because the item is heavy, show-floor timing matters, and decorator receiving is set up for it.
probes.label_rationale: The cited sessions distinguish small hotel-held packages from demo cases, decorator shipments, contractor-trailer kits, and plant dock reroutes. Houston's heavy show-floor crate matches the decorator case rather than the hotel cases.
probes.query: Houston trade show: an 80-pound demo crate and monitor stand must be on the show floor before the user lands. The decorator has dock hours and advance labels; a distributor branch could sign but would require a courier, and the hotel accepts only small parcels. Which shipping policy fits?

choices.text: Ship the sampling kit to the contractor trailer with the site contact and dock-hour window.
Ship it to the hotel under the reservation so it is waiting at check-in.
Always route plant-trip kits to the distributor branch, even when the site trailer can sign.
Carry the kit on the flight and skip all advance receiving for site visits.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hotel, branch, and carry-on policies each echo plausible prior outcomes. The chosen policy avoids a fixed receiver and uses the kit location, signing window, and Thursday availability requirement.
probes.gold_action: Send the Omaha sampling kit to the contractor trailer because it can sign during the needed window and is closest to the Thursday work.
probes.label_rationale: Cited shipments used hotels only for confirmed small packages, decorators for show materials, carry-on when appropriate, trailers for site kits, and docks when rerouted. Omaha's on-site trailer is the current receiver that protects the plant visit.
probes.query: Omaha plant visit: the sampling kit must be available Thursday morning. The contractor trailer on-site will sign Wednesday 8-4; the branch is across town and the hotel will accept only small guest parcels. Which receiving policy fits?
